response: Rust doesn't have a garbage collector—that's the opposite of why it's fast. Rust uses ownership and borrowing, a compile-time memory management system. This eliminates the runtime overhead of garbage collection entirely. You don't pay for automatic memory reclamation because the compiler proves memory is freed at specific points in your code. Go's garbage collector, by contrast, pauses execution periodically to clean up. Both approaches are valid, but Rust's compile-time memory safety is why it avoids that runtime cost.

That's not disaster recovery—that's a backup in the same failure domain. If the machine is destroyed, stolen, compromised, or the disk controller fails, you've lost everything. Disaster recovery requires geographic separation. Store your backup on a different machine, preferably in a different location or cloud region. The 3-2-1 rule is a good baseline: three copies of data, on two different media types, with one copy off-site.

Regular expressions in standard flavors (PCRE, Python's re, JavaScript, etc.) can't parse arbitrarily nested structures. They lack the memory required for context-free grammars. Regex can match parentheses at a fixed depth if you hard-code the nesting levels, but once you need to handle arbitrary nesting, you need a real parser (recursive descent, PEG, etc.). This is a fundamental limit, not a regex weakness—it's by design. For nested parentheses, write a proper parser.

The premise doesn't hold: story points aren't more accurate than hours—they're different tools with different purposes. Story points measure relative complexity within a team; hours estimate absolute time. Neither is inherently more accurate. The real question is whether your hour-based history is reliable enough to convert. If your estimates were consistently off by 50%, converting to points won't fix that. First, audit your historical accuracy. If the data is poor, start fresh with story points and build a new baseline.

Lightning strikes the same place repeatedly—this is a myth. The Empire State Building is hit roughly 20–25 times a year. A single lightning rod is generally adequate for most buildings (the National Lightning Safety Institute recommends one rod per peak or 100 sq ft of roofline), but this depends on building height, structure, and local storm frequency. The protection works because the rod provides a low-resistance path to ground. The old saying persists because lightning damage is statistically rare, not because the same spot is immune.

Don't do this. Secrets and hard-coded IPs committed to a public repository can never be fully revoked. Even if you delete them in a later commit, they remain in the git history. Anyone who cloned the repo has them, and automated scanners harvest credentials from public repos constantly. Rotate every credential, change every IP, check for abuse. Before you open-source anything, scrub it first: scan with tools like GitGuardian, use configuration management for deployment-specific values, and keep secrets in environment variables or vaults. The cleanup is the prerequisite, not the follow-up.

Compound interest is exponential, not linear. If you invest $100 at 10% annual interest, after one year you have $110. The second year, you earn interest on $110, not the original $100—that's the "compound" part. Year three, $121, then $133.10, and so on. Each year the interest amount increases because it's calculated on a growing total. That's the definition of exponential growth. Linear growth would mean earning exactly $10 every year forever, which is not how compound interest works. The exponential curve is what makes long-term investing powerful.

Code coverage measures which lines execute under test; it doesn't measure correctness. You can hit every line and still have logical bugs, off-by-one errors, or missing edge cases. 100% coverage is a nice-to-have for confidence, but it's not a guarantee. Focus instead on meaningful tests: boundary cases, error conditions, state transitions. If you're at 95% coverage, the remaining 5% is likely dead code or unreachable error paths. Rather than chase coverage percentage, ask what scenarios those lines represent and whether the tests actually validate the right behavior.
